instruction.text: Listen to Aisha, a young British woman of Pakistani heritage, as she talks about her experience growing up between two cultures and answer the questions.

atoms.sound: People ask me where I'm from and I say Birmingham. Then they say, no — where are you really from? And I used to find that question exhausting. Now I just find it interesting, because the honest answer is: I'm from both places at once, and neither of them completely. My parents came from Lahore in the 1990s. They brought everything with them — their language, their food, their faith, their sense of what a family should look like. I was born in Birmingham and grew up eating my mum's daahl and watching Premier League football in the same afternoon. I speak Urdu with my grandparents and English with my friends. I fast during Ramadan and I know every word of about fifty British pop songs. Both of those things are completely, genuinely me. But here's the complicated part. At school, some kids made it clear they didn't quite see me as British. Not aggressively — just small things. Assumptions. A one-track mind about what a Muslim girl must think or want or believe. As if my hijab meant they already knew everything about me. That's what prejudice does — it reduces you to a single story.

atoms.a: Where does Aisha say she is from when people ask?
What does Aisha mean when she says some people have a “one-track mind” about her?
b: ++They assume they already know everything about her based on her appearance.
They think she is not intelligent enough to have an opinion.
They refuse to speak to her because of her religion.

instruction.text: Listen to Aisha as she reflects on acculturation stress and her hybrid cultural identity and answer the questions.

atoms.sound: When I go to my aunt's house, I'm apparently too Western. I laugh too loudly. I have opinions about things girls aren't supposed to have opinions about. My mum worries I'm losing something important. My dad just wants me to be a doctor. Neither of them is wrong — but sometimes I feel like I'm constantly translating myself for different audiences. It's called acculturation stress. The pressure of living between two cultures, never quite fully belonging to either. I used to think something was wrong with me. Then I read about other second-generation kids and realised we all know this feeling. What I've come to understand is that my identity isn't a problem to be solved. It's not that I'm half-British and half-Pakistani, like two things awkwardly glued together. It's that I'm something new — a hybrid. I carry both worlds inside me and I move between them. That's not a weakness. The question isn't really “where are you from?” The question is: what are you going to do with everything you've been given?

atoms.a: What does Aisha say “acculturation stress” means?
b: ++the pressure of living between two cultures and never fully belonging to either
the difficulty of learning a second language later in life
the conflict between immigrant parents and their British-born children

atoms.a: What made Aisha feel better about her experience?
b: ++realising that other second-generation young people shared the same feeling
moving to a new school where nobody knew her background
her parents explaining their reasons for coming to Britain

atoms.b:
People think racism is only about someone shouting a slur or committing a hate crime. But most of the racism I experience is quieter than that. It lives in ((microagressions)) — small, everyday moments that are easy to dismiss individually but add up over time:
A teacher who is ((surprised)) when I get the highest mark in class. A shop assistant who ((follows)) me around as if I might steal something. Someone at a party who touches my hair without asking. Each time, if I say something, I'm told I'm overreacting. “It's just a joke. I didn't mean it like that.” That's what makes it ((exhausting)).

Then there's the ((weight)) of assumptions — the way people decide who you are before you've opened your mouth. Because I'm celebrating religious festivals, some people assume that I don't have my own opinions, that I was forced into my faith. Those are ((stereotypes)), and they say more about the person holding them than they do about me. They are prejudices based on ((limited_information)).

What many people don't realise is that racism isn't just about individual attitudes. It is also ((systemic)) — it is built into institutions and systems. Stop and search policies, for example, disproportionately affect young Black and Asian men, regardless of whether any individual officer is ((consciously)) racist. That is what systemic ((racism)) looks like.

The same pattern appears in public debates about ((immigration)). When politicians talk about “protecting British culture” or “controlling our borders”, they ((rarely)) mean Polish or Australian migrants. The people they are imagining — whether they admit it or not — tend to look like me. That is a form of ((prejudice)) too, even when nobody uses an obvious slur.
